subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Replication makes exact copies, and every dividing cell needs it
Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
Strands have 5' and 3' ends, and polymerase builds one way only
Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
Codon and anticodon pair by complementary bases
Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
Many polypeptides are cut or altered before they work
Three kinds of gene mutation: substitution, insertion, deletion
Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
Mutation is where all new alleles come from
CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it

questions.q: A cut in the skin heals as new skin cells are produced by cell division. Why must DNA replication take place before each of these divisions?
options: So that each new cell receives a complete copy of the DNA with an identical base sequence.
So that the existing DNA can be divided equally, half going to each of the new cells.
It does not need to take place, because replication is only required for reproduction.
So that the original DNA can stay intact in one cell and the other cell gets a new copy.
optionWhy: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.
A student who thinks division shares out the DNA picks this. The DNA is copied before division so that each new cell receives a complete set, not half of the original.

A student who links replication only with reproduction picks this. Replication is also required for growth and tissue replacement in multicellular organisms, since each new cell needs a full copy of the DNA.
A student who imagines conservative replication picks this. Each daughter molecule contains one original strand and one new strand, so neither cell receives the intact original molecule.
questions.explain: DNA replication produces exact copies of DNA with identical base sequences. It is required not only for reproduction but for growth and tissue replacement, because every cell produced by division must receive a complete copy.

questions.q: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?
options: It cuts through the sugar–phosphate backbone so that the two strands can come apart.
It adds free nucleotides to each exposed template strand to assemble the two new strands.
It forms the hydrogen bonds that hold each new nucleotide to its complementary base on the template.
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands.
optionWhy: A student who thinks helicase cuts the DNA picks this. Helicase breaks only the hydrogen bonds between bases; the covalent backbone of each strand stays intact so that it can act as a template.
A student who has swapped the two enzymes picks this. Assembling the new strands is the general role of DNA polymerase, not of helicase.
A student who believes an enzyme must make the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase breaks hydrogen bonds rather than forming them.
Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.
questions.explain: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.

questions.q: A forensic laboratory compares a sample from a crime scene with a suspect's DNA using 20 different markers rather than one. Why does this make the result more reliable?
options: One marker is already conclusive, because everyone's DNA is unique; extra markers only make the bands easier to read.
Testing 20 markers is equivalent to repeating a single marker 20 times, and repeating a measurement makes it more accurate.
Each extra independent marker multiplies down the chance that an unrelated person matches by coincidence.
With 20 markers the whole base sequence of the suspect's genome is read, so the identification is made complete.
optionWhy: A student who transfers the uniqueness of a whole genome to a single marker picks this. Each marker is shared by a proportion of the population, so one marker gives many chance matches.

A student who reads 'more measurements' as 'repeat the same measurement' picks this. Repeating one marker gives the same lengths each time and does not change the chance that another person shares them.

The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.
A student who thinks profiling reads DNA sequences picks this. A profile compares fragment lengths at a small number of variable regions; it does not read the base sequence of the genome.
questions.explain: The chance that an unrelated person matches at one marker might be a few per cent; the chances at independent markers multiply together, so with 20 markers a false match becomes extremely improbable. This is the NOS principle that reliability is enhanced by increasing the number of measurements.

questions.q: During replication, how does DNA polymerase add each new nucleotide to the strand it is building?
options: It joins the 3' hydroxyl of the incoming nucleotide to the 5' terminal of the growing strand, so that the strand grows in the 3' to 5' direction.
It adds to whichever terminal faces the fork, so both new strands grow in the same direction as the replication fork moves.
It forms hydrogen bonds between the incoming nucleotide and the template base, which then hold the nucleotide in the strand.
It joins the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide to the 3' terminal of the growing strand, so the strand grows in the 5' to 3' direction.
optionWhy: A student who takes the direction the template is read as the direction of synthesis picks this. DNA polymerase can only add to the 3' terminal, so the new strand grows 5' to 3'.
A student who pictures the two strands as parallel picks this. The strands are antiparallel and DNA polymerase adds only to a 3' terminal, so only one new strand can grow towards the fork.

A student who thinks the enzyme makes the base pair picks this. The hydrogen bonds to the template form spontaneously; DNA polymerase forms the covalent bond that links the nucleotide's 5' phosphate to the 3' terminal of the strand.

The phosphate on the 5' carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the last nucleotide in the strand. Growth is therefore only at the 3' terminal, in the 5' to 3' direction, while the template is read 3' to 5'.
questions.explain: The phosphate on the 5' carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the last nucleotide in the strand. Growth is therefore only at the 3' terminal, in the 5' to 3' direction, while the template is read 3' to 5'.

questions.q: What is the function of DNA polymerase I in prokaryotic DNA replication?
options: It synthesizes most of the new DNA on both strands, being the first polymerase to act at the fork.
It joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of adjacent Okazaki fragments to make one continuous lagging strand.
It removes the RNA nucleotides of each primer and replaces them with DNA nucleotides, filling the gap.
It synthesizes the short DNA primer that DNA polymerase III needs at the start of each fragment.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'I' as the main enzyme picks this. The bulk of DNA synthesis on both strands is carried out by DNA polymerase III.
A student who blurs the polymerases with ligase picks this. Sealing the nick between fragments is the function of DNA ligase, which acts after DNA polymerase I has replaced the primer.
DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer and fills the gap with DNA nucleotides, extending the 3' terminal of the adjacent DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick.
A student who thinks the primer is DNA made by a DNA polymerase picks this. The primer is RNA, made by DNA primase; DNA polymerase I removes it rather than making it.
questions.explain: DNA polymerase I removes each RNA primer and fills the gap with DNA nucleotides, extending the 3' terminal of the adjacent DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick.

questions.q: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?
options: Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the enzyme bonds the RNA to the DNA picks this. RNA polymerase forms covalent bonds between successive RNA nucleotides along the backbone; base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds.
A student who expects a like-for-like copy picks this. Bases pair with their complements (A with U, C with G), so the RNA is complementary to the template, not identical to it.

Complementary base pairing between the RNA nucleotide and the template base is held by hydrogen bonds. These are weak and temporary, so the completed RNA separates from the DNA and the DNA strands re-pair.
A student who forgets that RNA contains uracil picks this. Adenine on the DNA template strand pairs with uracil on the RNA strand; there is no thymine in RNA.
questions.explain: Complementary base pairing between the RNA nucleotide and the template base is held by hydrogen bonds. These are weak and temporary, so the completed RNA separates from the DNA and the DNA strands re-pair.

questions.q: Why is transcription regarded as a key stage at which the expression of a gene can be switched on or off?
options: Every gene in a cell is transcribed and translated all the time, so expression is not switched on or off at any stage.
It is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide.
All genes in a cell are transcribed at all times, so expression is switched on and off only at translation.
It is the stage at which amino acids are assembled into a chain, so it decides which protein is made.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every gene is always expressed picks this. Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time; a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide, so transcription is the stage that is switched on and off.

Transcription is the first stage of gene expression. If a gene is not transcribed there is no mRNA, so nothing further in the expression of that gene can happen; switching transcription on or off switches the gene on or off.

A student who locates the control of expression at translation picks this. Not all genes are transcribed at any given time; because transcription is the first stage, switching it off stops the mRNA being made at all, so it is the key stage at which a gene is switched on or off.
A student who has swapped transcription and translation picks this. Amino acids are assembled in translation; transcription produces the mRNA and is the key control stage because it comes first.
questions.explain: Transcription is the first stage of gene expression. If a gene is not transcribed there is no mRNA, so nothing further in the expression of that gene can happen; switching transcription on or off switches the gene on or off.

questions.q: What happens during translation?
options: A base sequence of DNA is used as a template to make a complementary mRNA molecule inside the cell nucleus.
Ribosomes convert the bases of the mRNA into amino acids, which are then joined into a chain.
The base sequence of an mRNA molecule is used to determine the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Amino acids are joined into a polypeptide inside the nucleus, right beside the DNA of the gene that codes for it.
optionWhy: A student who has swapped the two terms picks this. Making mRNA on a DNA template is transcription; translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from the mRNA.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. The amino acids already exist in the cytoplasm and are brought by tRNA; the mRNA only determines the order in which they are joined.
Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.
A student who keeps the whole process in the nucleus picks this. Translation takes place on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA has left the nucleus.
questions.explain: Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.

questions.q: The start codon on an mRNA molecule is AUG. Which tRNA anticodon binds to this codon, and how is it held there?
options: AUG, the same three bases as the codon
UAC, held to the codon by hydrogen bonds
TAC, with thymine pairing to adenine
UAC, bonded to the codon by covalent bonds
optionWhy: A student who reads 'matching' as 'identical' picks this. The anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing, so it is UAC, not AUG.
The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C, giving UAC. The codon and anticodon are held together by hydrogen bonds, which break when the tRNA leaves.
A student who applies the DNA pairing rules picks this. tRNA is RNA and contains uracil, not thymine, so the base that pairs with the A of the codon is U.

A student who thinks the ribosome bonds the tRNA to the mRNA picks this. Codon and anticodon pair by hydrogen bonds, which must break so the tRNA can leave; covalent bonds form only between amino acids.
questions.explain: The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A pairs with U, U with A and G with C, giving UAC. The codon and anticodon are held together by hydrogen bonds, which break when the tRNA leaves.

questions.q: Part of an mRNA molecule, written in the order in which it is translated, has the base sequence AUGGGCAACAGA. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine, GGC glycine, AAC asparagine, AGA arginine, UAC tyrosine, CCG proline, UUG leucine, UCU serine, UGG tryptophan, GCA alanine, ACA threonine. Which amino acid is the third in the polypeptide?
options: arginine
asparagine
leucine
threonine
optionWhy: A student who treats AUG as a start signal only, and begins counting from GGC, makes arginine (AGA) the third amino acid. AUG codes for methionine, which is the first amino acid, so the third is asparagine.
Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.

A student who first writes the complementary sequence (UAC CCG UUG UCU) and looks that up picks leucine. The table is for mRNA codons and the sequence given is already mRNA, so no complement should be taken.
A student who begins reading from the second base (UGG GCA ACA) picks threonine. The reading frame is fixed by the start codon AUG, so codons must be counted from the first base.
questions.explain: Reading from the start codon in groups of three gives AUG GGC AAC AGA: methionine, glycine, asparagine, arginine. The third codon, AAC, codes for asparagine.

questions.q: How is the polypeptide chain lengthened during translation?
options: All the tRNAs first line up along the whole length of the mRNA, and their amino acids are then joined together in one step.
Each tRNA stays attached to its own amino acid, so the chain is a series of tRNAs joined through their amino acids.
Each new amino acid is held to the previous one by hydrogen bonds, like those between codon and anticodon.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and a peptide bond links each new amino acid to the chain.
optionWhy: A student who takes a diagram of many tRNAs literally picks this. Only two tRNAs are on the ribosome at once, and amino acids are added one at a time as the ribosome moves.
A student who leaves the tRNAs in the chain picks this. Each tRNA is released once its amino acid has been joined by a peptide bond, and the chain consists of amino acids only.
A student who generalizes hydrogen bonding to the whole topic picks this. Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, which are covalent; hydrogen bonds hold codon to anticodon only temporarily.

Elongation is stepwise: the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, a tRNA pairs with each codon in turn, and the amino acid it carries is linked to the growing polypeptide by a peptide bond.
questions.explain: Elongation is stepwise: the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, a tRNA pairs with each codon in turn, and the amino acid it carries is linked to the growing polypeptide by a peptide bond.

questions.q: Which statement about the direction of translation is correct?
options: The ribosome can begin at either end of the mRNA, since the start codon is recognized wherever it is met.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 5' end towards its 3' end, so the codon nearest the 5' end is translated first.
The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 3' end towards its 5' end, matching the direction the template is read.
The ribosome begins at the 5' cap and translates every base up to and including the poly-A tail at the 3' end.
optionWhy: A student who gives the mRNA no direction picks this. The ribosome binds at the 5' end and moves towards the 3' end; it does not begin from the 3' end.

Translation is 5' to 3': the small subunit binds near the 5' end of the mRNA, finds the start codon and the ribosome moves towards the 3' end, so the polypeptide is built from the 5'-most codon onward.
A student who transfers the 3' to 5' reading of the DNA template to the mRNA picks this. The mRNA is read in its own 5' to 3' direction, the same direction in which it was synthesized.
A student who treats the whole mRNA as code picks this. Translation runs 5' to 3' but only from the start codon to the stop codon; the cap and tail are not translated.
questions.explain: Translation is 5' to 3': the small subunit binds near the 5' end of the mRNA, finds the start codon and the ribosome moves towards the 3' end, so the polypeptide is built from the 5'-most codon onward.

questions.q: What is the role of the 5' cap and the 3' poly-A tail added to a eukaryotic mRNA transcript?
options: They are translated, adding a short run of extra amino acids to each end of the polypeptide.
They stabilize the mRNA, protecting it from being broken down before it is translated.
They mark the positions of the introns so that the splicing enzymes know which sections to remove.
They have no function, being left over from transcription of non-coding DNA at each end of the gene.
optionWhy: A student who assumes every part of the mRNA is code picks this. Translation runs from the start codon to the stop codon; the cap and tail lie outside this and add no amino acids.
The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added after transcription to stabilize mRNA transcripts, so that the mRNA survives to be exported from the nucleus and translated.
A student who muddles the modifications picks this. The cap and tail are at the two ends of the transcript; introns are internal and are recognized by their own sequences.
A student who equates non-coding with functionless picks this. The cap and tail are not transcribed from the gene at all; they are added afterwards and have the function of stabilizing the mRNA.
questions.explain: The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added after transcription to stabilize mRNA transcripts, so that the mRNA survives to be exported from the nucleus and translated.

questions.q: Which sequence of events initiates translation of an mRNA in a eukaryotic cell?
options: The complete ribosome binds directly to the start codon as a single unit, and the initiator tRNA then enters the ribosome and pairs with the codon.
The small subunit binds to the 3' end of the mRNA and moves along until it reaches the start codon, where the large subunit attaches.
The small subunit binds at the start codon, and the initiator tRNA enters at the E site before the large subunit attaches to it.
The small subunit binds to the 5' end of the mRNA and moves to the start codon; the initiator tRNA binds there; then the large subunit attaches.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the ribosome as a single unit picks this. The small subunit binds first, at the 5' end, and the large subunit attaches only after the initiator tRNA is in place at the start codon.
A student who gives the mRNA no direction picks this. The small subunit attaches to the 5' terminal of the mRNA and moves towards the 3' end to find the start codon.
A student who reads E as 'entry' picks this. The initiator tRNA occupies the P site once the large subunit has attached; the E site is the exit site from which used tRNAs leave.

Initiation begins with attachment of the small ribosomal subunit to the 5' terminal of the mRNA. It moves to the start codon, the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with AUG, and the large subunit then attaches so that a second tRNA can enter the A site.
questions.explain: Initiation begins with attachment of the small ribosomal subunit to the 5' terminal of the mRNA. It moves to the start codon, the initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with AUG, and the large subunit then attaches so that a second tRNA can enter the A site.

questions.q: Insulin consists of two polypeptide chains, A and B, held together by disulfide bonds, yet it is coded for by a single gene. How is functional insulin produced?
options: Two separate polypeptides, A and B, are translated from the gene and are then joined to each other by disulfide bonds in the Golgi apparatus.
Pre-proinsulin loses its signal sequence to give proinsulin; a central section is then cut out, leaving the two chains.
The polypeptide made by translation is already insulin, and the two chains form as it folds when it leaves the ribosome.
Alternative splicing of the insulin pre-mRNA produces two different mature mRNAs, one of which codes for each of the two chains.
optionWhy: A student who explains two chains by two polypeptides picks this. One polypeptide is translated; the two chains are what remains of it after a central section is removed.

This is the two-stage modification of pre-proinsulin: removal of the signal sequence gives proinsulin, which folds and forms disulfide bonds, and removal of the central section then leaves the A and B chains joined as active insulin.
A student who thinks translation makes the finished protein picks this. Pre-proinsulin is not functional; two sections must be removed before it becomes insulin.
A student who over-applies alternative splicing picks this. The two chains of insulin are not splice variants; they are two parts of a single polypeptide cut after translation.
questions.explain: This is the two-stage modification of pre-proinsulin: removal of the signal sequence gives proinsulin, which folds and forms disulfide bonds, and removal of the central section then leaves the A and B chains joined as active insulin.

questions.q: Part of the base sequence of a gene is GAT TCA GGC ATT before a mutation and GAT TCG GCA TT after it. Which type of gene mutation has occurred?
options: A deletion of one base, which has moved every later base one position along
A substitution of the base A by G at the sixth position in the sequence
A chromosome mutation, because the total amount of DNA has changed
A substitution that has shifted the reading frame of later codons
optionWhy: Aligning the two sequences shows that the A in the second codon is missing and every base after it has moved up one place; the mutant is one base shorter. This is a deletion.

A student who compares the sequences position by position sees A become G and calls it a substitution. A substitution leaves the length unchanged, but the mutant sequence has 11 bases instead of 12: one base has been deleted and the rest have shifted.

A student who sorts mutations by whether DNA is gained or lost picks this. A change of one base within a gene is a gene mutation (a deletion); chromosome mutations alter the number or structure of whole chromosomes.

A student who attaches frameshift to every mutation picks this. The frame has shifted, but only because a base was removed; a substitution cannot shift the frame because it does not change the number of bases.
questions.explain: Aligning the two sequences shows that the A in the second codon is missing and every base after it has moved up one place; the mutant is one base shorter. This is a deletion.

questions.q: Which statement about the causes of gene mutation is correct?
options: Gene mutations arise only in cells that are exposed to a mutagen
Microwaves and radio waves are mutagenic just like X-rays
Replication errors can cause mutation without a mutagen
Proofreading by DNA polymerase corrects every error
optionWhy: A student who knows mutagens as the cause of mutation picks this. Mutagens raise the rate, but replication and repair errors produce a background rate of mutation in cells that have met no mutagen at all.

A student who treats all radiation as dangerous to DNA picks this. Only ionizing radiation, such as X-rays and gamma rays, and ultraviolet light have enough energy to alter DNA; microwaves and radio waves do not.

Gene mutation is caused by mutagens and by errors in DNA replication or repair. DNA polymerase occasionally pairs a base wrongly, and a small fraction of these errors escape proofreading and repair and become permanent mutations.
A student who turns a very low error rate into a zero error rate picks this. Proofreading and repair correct most errors, but not all, which is why replication errors are a genuine cause of mutation.
questions.explain: Gene mutation is caused by mutagens and by errors in DNA replication or repair. DNA polymerase occasionally pairs a base wrongly, and a small fraction of these errors escape proofreading and repair and become permanent mutations.

questions.q: Which statement about mutations in germ cells and somatic cells is correct?
options: A mutation in a skin cell can be inherited by the person's children
Every mutation in a somatic cell causes that cell to become cancerous
A mutation in a germ cell can be passed on to the offspring
A mutation in one liver cell spreads to every body cell
optionWhy: A student who treats all of a person's DNA as heritable picks this. Skin cells are somatic cells: their DNA is never passed to a gamete, so the mutation dies with the individual.
A student who equates somatic mutation with cancer picks this. Cancer follows mutations in the genes that control the cell cycle; most somatic mutations are silent or harmless.

Germ cells give rise to gametes, so a mutated gene in a germ cell can be passed to the next generation, where it will be present in every cell of the offspring. This is how mutation adds inherited variation to a species.
A student who generalises from inherited mutations picks this. A somatic mutation is copied only into the descendants of the cell in which it occurred, not into other cells of the body.
questions.explain: Germ cells give rise to gametes, so a mutated gene in a germ cell can be passed to the next generation, where it will be present in every cell of the offspring. This is how mutation adds inherited variation to a species.

questions.q: Why is gene mutation described as the original source of all genetic variation?
options: New alleles arise only by mutation; meiosis and fertilization just recombine alleles that already exist
Crossing over in meiosis creates new alleles, and mutation adds to the variation they produce
Most mutations are beneficial, so each one adds a useful new variant to the species
Organisms generate new alleles whenever their environment demands a new trait from them
optionWhy: Every allele of every gene began as a mutation in a germ cell of some ancestor. Meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of alleles, which adds variation among individuals, but they cannot produce a new allele.
A student who thinks crossing over makes new genes picks this. Crossing over exchanges existing alleles between chromatids; it produces new combinations, not new alleles.

A student who thinks mutation is mostly helpful picks this. Most mutations are harmful or neutral for the individual; mutation is the source of variation regardless of whether a particular mutation is useful.
A student who believes mutation is directed picks this. Mutations occur at random with respect to their usefulness; the environment selects among variants that already exist.
questions.explain: Every allele of every gene began as a mutation in a germ cell of some ancestor. Meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of alleles, which adds variation among individuals, but they cannot produce a new allele.

questions.q: In CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, what determines the position in the genome at which the DNA is cut?
options: The base sequence of the guide RNA, which pairs with the complementary sequence in the target DNA
The active site of the Cas9 enzyme, which recognises the target DNA base sequence directly
The guide RNA, which cuts both strands of the DNA at the position where it binds to it
The sequence of the new bases that Cas9 itself inserts into the gene to rewrite it
optionWhy: The guide RNA contains about 20 bases complementary to the target. Base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA holds Cas9 at that one position, where Cas9 cuts both strands. Changing the guide RNA sequence changes the site that is cut.
A student who expects specificity to come from the enzyme picks this. Cas9 cuts wherever it is taken; the target is chosen by the guide RNA, not by the enzyme's active site.
A student who gives the guide RNA the active role picks this. The guide RNA does locate the target, but it cannot cut DNA; the enzyme Cas9 makes the cut.
A student who thinks Cas9 writes the new sequence picks this. Cas9 only cuts; any new sequence is copied in by the cell's repair processes, and the cut site is set by the guide RNA.
questions.explain: The guide RNA contains about 20 bases complementary to the target. Base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA holds Cas9 at that one position, where Cas9 cuts both strands. Changing the guide RNA sequence changes the site that is cut.
